metadata.note: STEM explainer on the claude-hai channel: what real per-minute web traffic looks like (daily cycle, noise, one-minute bursts, repeats), why it matters for autoscaling, and what it means for anyone testing on made-up traffic. Every curve is real data from the Azure Functions 2019 trace except the B07 'made-up traffic' panel, which is labelled as a redrawn illustration.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW: the writer types the misconception (smooth and steady) and corrects it (noisy and jumpy).
beats.narration_text: Real web traffic is noisy and jumpy, but it repeats every day. Test a system on smooth, made-up traffic, and you test it against traffic that does not exist.

beats.role_note: the slow part: one real app, minute by minute, three days
beats.narration_text: Here is one real web app from Microsoft's public Azure Functions trace, minute by minute, for three days. Traffic rises and falls once a day. That daily cycle is the slow, easy part.
beats.new_visual_element: three days of real per-minute requests, with day boundaries

show.event: Azure logo and credit; axes for requests per minute over three days
the real trace draws on, minute by minute
a smooth hourly average traces the daily cycle over it

shot.visual_intent: App 9aba8d35, days 2-4, unscaled requests per minute (evidence.json hero3_min).

beats.role_note: the fast part: one calm hour bounces about 15% around its recent median
beats.narration_text: Zoom in to one hour and it is never smooth. From one minute to the next, load jumps around by about fifteen percent, even when nothing special is happening.
beats.new_visual_element: one real hour, minute bars around a 30-minute median with a 15% band

show.event: 60 real per-minute values land one by one
the trailing 30-minute median draws through them
a band of plus or minus 15% appears; most minutes sit inside it, none sit still

beats.role_note: bursts: about 24 per app per day, about 1.9 times normal, one minute long, 72% peak in their first minute, about a third rise the minute before
beats.narration_text: Then there are bursts. A typical app sees about twenty-four a day. A typical burst is almost twice the normal load and lasts one minute. Seventy-two percent hit their peak in the very first minute, and only about a third rise at all in the minute before.
beats.new_visual_element: three real one-minute bursts and four measured numbers

show.event: three real bursts, each drawn relative to its normal load, jump in one minute
counter: about 24 bursts per app per day
counter: 1.9 times normal load, 1 minute long
counter: 72% peak in the first minute
counter: about 1 in 3 rise the minute before

shot.visual_intent: Bursts from apps e7a26f46, e8cb71e1, ec941895 (evidence.json burst_examples); numbers from demo_stdout.txt and evidence.json rise_before.

beats.role_note: bursts repeat at the same time of day: app 9aba8d35, 73% of bursts return within 5 minutes on another day
beats.narration_text: But many bursts come back at the same time of day. In one app, seventy-three percent of bursts return at the same time on another day. Random timing would give far fewer.
beats.new_visual_element: burst times over ten real days, against the same number at random times

show.event: ten rows, one per day; each real burst lands as a dot at its time of day
the dots stack into columns; counter 73% repeat
a second panel scatters the same number of dots at random times (constructed comparison)

beats.role_note: three answers for autoscaling, measured on 5 held-out apps, 65 unseen days
beats.narration_text: For autoscaling, this decides the plan. Reacting is too slow for one-minute bursts. Keeping spare servers all day works, but costs about twice as much. Planning from yesterday's pattern gets most of the benefit for far less.
beats.new_visual_element: react, spare capacity, yesterday: late requests and cost side by side

show.event: React (Kubernetes rule): late bar grows to 5.47%, cost bar to 19,986
Spare capacity (fixed for the day's peak): 0.07% late, cost 39,445
Plan from yesterday: 1.17% late, cost 24,488

beats.role_note: made-up traffic was too smooth (5% noise, ramps); real is about 15% and jumps; the fitted generator copies real statistics (16%, 1.81x, 67%)
beats.narration_text: My first, made-up traffic used five percent noise and bursts that ramped up slowly. Real traffic has about fifteen percent noise and jumps in one minute. So I built a generator that copies each real app's statistics. Its noise is sixteen percent, and two thirds of its bursts peak in the first minute. Close to real.
beats.new_visual_element: one day each: made-up (redrawn), real, fitted generator

show.event: a smooth day with a slow ramped burst, labelled 'made-up (redrawn): 5% noise, ramped burst'
a real day draws beneath it: about 15% noise, jumps
the fitted generator's day draws third: noise 16%, 67% peak in first minute

shot.visual_intent: Made-up panel is a constructed illustration (real daily shape + 5% noise + 10-minute ramp), labelled as redrawn; real = app 9aba8d35 day 4; fitted = FittedTraffic(train_series()) seed 3 (evidence.json compare).

beats.role_note: recap card; the narration carries the takeaway
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Before you trust a test, measure your real traffic: its noise, its bursts per day, and how fast they peak. Then make your test traffic match.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW: the prompt is read aloud verbatim, then discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Here are two weeks of my service's requests per minute. Measure the minute-to-minute noise, count the bursts per day, and tell me how many peak in their first minute. Then compare those three numbers with your test traffic.

cli_exercise.ask: Here are two weeks of my service's requests per minute. Measure the minute-to-minute noise, count the bursts per day, and tell me how many peak in their first minute.
cli_exercise.output_description: Three numbers for the real traffic: noise level, bursts per day, share of bursts that peak in their first minute.
cli_exercise.change: Run the same three measurements on the traffic your load tests use.
cli_exercise.output2_description: The same three numbers for the test traffic, side by side; large gaps mean the test is easier than reality.
cli_exercise.next_step: Run it on your own service's per-minute request log and your load-test traffic.
